header.question:
A document in the library contains this sentence:

> Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are almost always polysemantic, with nearly every neuron activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020).

Check what the sentence says about the work it cites against that work in the library. Does the cited source support it? Cite the page(s) of the cited source that show what it actually says.

args.query: Using individual neurons as these units has had some success

events.error: quote too short to check: it needs at least 10 letters or digits. A term that short is a search, not a quotation: use search instead.

args.quote: Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs.

args.text:
Verdict: not supported

This is a test.

Verdict: not supported

In *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits*, Olah et al. state that "Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62). They do not claim that neurons are "almost always polysemantic" or that nearly every neuron is polysemantic. In fact, they write that "the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22). Furthermore, in *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models*, the original text actually reads: "Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020)" (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p1).

Verdict: not supported

The cited document, *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits*, does not support the claim that neurons are almost always polysemantic or that nearly every neuron activates for several unrelated types of feature.

Instead, Olah et al. state that "Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62). Rather than claiming that polysemanticity affects nearly every neuron, they observe that "thousands of hours of studying individual neurons have led us to believe the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22). While they note that "polysemantic neurons are a major challenge for the circuits agenda, significantly limiting our ability to reason about neural networks" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65), they also describe instances where a model has a "“pure neuron”" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b97) before features are spread across other neurons in superposition.

In the library document where this sentence originates, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models*, the actual text does not make the extreme claim either; it states: "Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020)" (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p1).

Verdict: not supported

The cited work, *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits* by Olah et al. (2020), does not support the claim that neurons are almost always polysemantic or that nearly every neuron activates for several unrelated types of feature.

What Olah et al. actually state is that neural networks "often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62). Furthermore, they explicitly state that "thousands of hours of studying individual neurons have led us to believe the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22). While they emphasize that "polysemantic neurons are a major challenge for the circuits agenda, significantly limiting our ability to reason about neural networks" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65), they do not state or suggest that nearly every neuron is polysemantic.

The document in the library containing this discussion, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models*, accurately reflects the cited source by stating: "Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020)" (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p1).
